scenes.tts: A microphone in a healthy ear canal can record sound the cochlea itself made. Where does it come from?
scenes.visual: Title card: A Gain That Death Erases. A sealed ear canal with a small microphone; a faint wave travels outward from the inner ear. Question on screen: where does that sound come from?
scenes.narration: A microphone in a healthy ear canal can record sound the cochlea itself made. Where does it come from?

scenes.tts: Start with a cochlea that has no help. Sound sets up a travelling wave along the basilar membrane.
scenes.visual: A schematic cochlea uncoils into a long strip labelled basilar membrane, base at left, apex at right. A wave starts at the base.
scenes.narration: Start with a cochlea that has no help. Sound sets up a travelling wave along the basilar membrane.

scenes.tts: In a living ear, at soft levels, each place moves most for one frequency, its characteristic frequency. The wave peaks there and dies out just beyond.
scenes.visual: Tick labels along the strip: high frequencies at the base, low at the apex. The wave envelope grows, peaks at one place and collapses just past it. Label: characteristic frequency (living, soft levels).
scenes.narration: In a living ear, at soft levels, each place moves most for one frequency, its characteristic frequency. The wave peaks there and dies out just beyond.

scenes.tts: After death the wave remains, but weak and broadly tuned, and its peak can shift.
scenes.visual: The same strip in grey, labelled passive (after death). A low, broad peak, sitting slightly off the living peak.
scenes.narration: After death the wave remains, but weak and broadly tuned, and its peak can shift.

scenes.tts: Now pick one place. Play a tone at its characteristic frequency, and raise the level in steps.
scenes.visual: A dot marks one site near the base. Large axes fill the frame. x: sound level (dB). y: basilar-membrane motion (dB). Corner label: schematic, basal site.
scenes.narration: Now pick one place. Play a tone at its characteristic frequency, and raise the level in steps.

scenes.tts: After death, ten decibels more sound gives ten decibels more motion. That straight line is linear.
scenes.caption: After death, 10 dB more sound gives 10 dB more motion. That straight line is linear.
scenes.visual: A grey straight line draws, slope 1. Annotation: +10 dB in, +10 dB out. Labels: after death; linear.
scenes.narration: After death, 10 dB more sound gives 10 dB more motion. That straight line is linear.

scenes.tts: Predict. Where does the living ear differ most from the dead one, at soft levels or loud ones?
scenes.visual: The grey line alone. Two arrows: soft (left end) and loud (right end), each with a question mark. Text: Predict.
scenes.narration: Predict. Where does the living ear differ most from the dead one, at soft levels or loud ones?

scenes.tts: At soft levels. A soft tone moves the living membrane tens of decibels more.
scenes.visual: A gold living curve draws from the left, far above the grey line. A bracket at the left end: tens of dB.
scenes.narration: At soft levels. A soft tone moves the living membrane tens of decibels more.

scenes.tts: As the tone gets louder, the living response grows slowly, often two to five decibels for every ten.
scenes.caption: As the tone gets louder, the living response grows slowly, often 2 to 5 dB for every 10.
scenes.visual: The gold curve bends over into a shallow slope. Annotation: often 2 to 5 dB per 10 dB.
scenes.narration: As the tone gets louder, the living response grows slowly, often 2 to 5 dB for every 10.

scenes.tts: At the loudest levels, the two curves come close together.
scenes.visual: The gold curve approaches the grey line at the right.
scenes.narration: At the loudest levels, the two curves come close together.

scenes.tts: The gap between the curves is the cochlear amplifier. In mammals, it depends on outer hair cells.
scenes.visual: The gap between gold and grey shades and is labelled gain (the cochlear amplifier). An outer hair cell icon appears beside it.
scenes.narration: The gap between the curves is the cochlear amplifier. In mammals, it depends on outer hair cells.

scenes.tts: The gain is large only near the characteristic frequency, so it sharpens the peak as well as raising it.
scenes.visual: Back to the strip: the living wave peak is taller and narrower than the grey passive peak.
scenes.narration: The gain is large only near the characteristic frequency, so it sharpens the peak as well as raising it.

scenes.tts: Here is the one idea. Outer hair cells add energy to the wave near its peak.
scenes.visual: Card header: The one idea. Text builds: outer hair cells add energy near the peak.
scenes.narration: Here is the one idea. Outer hair cells add energy to the wave near its peak.

scenes.tts: The gain they give is large for soft sounds, small for loud ones, and gone after death.
scenes.visual: Three small gain bars: soft (tall), loud (short), after death (none). Small label: gain = living compared with dead.
scenes.narration: The gain they give is large for soft sounds, small for loud ones, and gone after death.

scenes.tts: Sensitivity, sharp tuning, compressive growth and the returning sound are four signatures of that one gain.
scenes.visual: Four labelled arrows come off the shaded gap: sensitivity, sharp tuning, compressive growth of motion, emissions.
scenes.narration: Sensitivity, sharp tuning, compressive growth and the returning sound are four signatures of that one gain.

scenes.tts: At the very softest levels, the gain stops rising. It levels off at its maximum.
scenes.visual: The far left of the gold curve runs parallel to the grey line. Label: plateau, gain at its maximum.
scenes.narration: At the very softest levels, the gain stops rising. It levels off at its maximum.

scenes.tts: Why want a gain that shrinks? Suppose the response grows two and a half decibels for every ten.
scenes.caption: Why want a gain that shrinks? Suppose the response grows 2.5 dB for every 10.
scenes.visual: The middle of the gold curve highlighted. Annotation: 2.5 dB per 10 dB, slope 0.25.
scenes.narration: Why want a gain that shrinks? Suppose the response grows 2.5 dB for every 10.

scenes.tts: If that slope held over sixty decibels, a quiet room to a shout would fit into fifteen decibels of motion.
scenes.caption: If that slope held over 60 dB, a quiet room to a shout would fit into 15 dB of motion.
scenes.visual: A wide input bar (60 dB, quiet room to shout) funnels into a short output bar. On screen: 60 x 0.25 = 15 dB. Footnote: illustrative slope, assumed constant.
scenes.narration: If that slope held over 60 dB, a quiet room to a shout would fit into 15 dB of motion.

scenes.tts: That is a thousandfold range of sound pressure, fitted into less than a sixfold range of motion.
scenes.visual: The two bars relabelled: input, 1000 times in pressure; output, under 6 times in motion. No noise-floor or limit lines.
scenes.narration: That is a thousandfold range of sound pressure, fitted into less than a sixfold range of motion.

scenes.tts: Outer hair cells push with a motor protein in their side wall, called prestin. How does a cell push that fast?
scenes.visual: An outer hair cell enlarges, prestin dots in its side wall, labelled prestin. Question: how does a cell push that fast?
scenes.narration: Outer hair cells push with a motor protein in their side wall, called prestin. How does a cell push that fast?

scenes.tts: Take this with you. The living cochlea adds a gain that is large for soft sounds, and death erases it.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: the living and dead curves, the gap shaded; text: a gain for soft sounds that death erases.
scenes.narration: Take this with you. The living cochlea adds a gain that is large for soft sounds, and death erases it.
